whup the daylights out of.meaning: To beat someone very hard as a punishment. ('Whup' is dialect for 'whip'; 'the daylights' is strong talk for 'very much.')

bite one's tongue.example: I got to bite my tongue not to let on about Shiloh.

bold as brass.example: "You got to treat a dog good if you want him to stick around," I say, bold as brass.
bold as brass.meaning: Very bold; not shy or afraid at all.

die of embarrassment.example: I blush then, 'cause my dad would die of embarrassment if he knew what Mr. Wallace is thinking-- that I'm buying this food for our supper, but there's no way in the world I can let on about Shiloh.

drive one nuts.example: Dara Lynn took only a nibble of hers every day or so, keeping it up on her dresser in its pink and yellow tinfoil, driving me nuts.

first thing out of one's mouth.example: "See my dog yet?" First thing out of his mouth.
forms: first thing out of his mouth

fix up.example: I fix him up some frankfurters, cut up and mixed with sour cream, and little chunks of cheese.
fix up.meaning: To prepare or cook food for someone.

get down on one's knees.example: But before I went to bed, when Ma asked me again about that rabbit, I gulped and said yes, and she made me get down on my knees and ask God's forgiveness, which wasn't so bad.
get down on one's knees.meaning: To kneel down, usually to pray.

give a lift.example: Somebody gave 'em a lift; you can always count on that around Friendly.
give a lift.meaning: To give someone a ride in a car.

happy as a flea on a dog.example: I'm happy as a flea on a dog.

head off.example: Next day, to head off David Howard from riding up from Friendly on his bike, I go down to see him.
head off.meaning: To stop something from happening before it starts.

hitch a ride.example: The walk to Friendly takes a good long time unless I hitch a ride.
hitch a ride.meaning: To get a free ride from someone driving by.

keep an eye out.example: Don't think you'll see much of him near the road, but you keep your eye out for him in the fields.

keep in mind.example: I hope you'll keep that in mind.

let on.example: I got to bite my tongue not to let on about Shiloh.
let on.meaning: To tell or show a secret.

smooth as buttermilk.example: Next two days go by smooth as buttermilk.
smooth as buttermilk.meaning: Going very easily, with no trouble at all.

throw a fit.example: Dara Lynn, of course, threw a fit, and when Ma asked me if I'd done it, I said no.
throw a fit.meaning: To suddenly show strong anger loudly; to lose control.

throw up.example: He throws up the first time he eats the stuff--too rich for his belly, I guess--but after that he manages to keep it down, and all the while he's fattening out a little.
throw up.meaning: To be sick; to bring food back up from the stomach.

wait it out.example: I want to jump up and scream, "No!" but I just grip my chair and wait it out.
wait it out.meaning: To wait calmly until a hard or dangerous time passes.

a warm spot in one's heart.example: All I can think of is to take Shiloh down to Friendly the next day, draw me up a big sign that says free-. world's best dog or something, and hold it up along the road to Sistersville, hoping that some stranger driving along will get a warm spot in his heart for Shiloh, stop his car, and take him home.
a warm spot in one's heart.meaning: A feeling of love or kindness for someone.

black and white.example: But it's not all so black and white as Dad makes it out to be, neither.
black and white.meaning: Clear and simple; easy to judge as right or wrong.

clear one's head.example: And sometimes, when I get mad, it clears my head.
clear one's head.meaning: To make one's mind calm and able to think well.

cross one's mind.example: I don't answer, because that very thing crossed my mind.
cross one's mind.meaning: To come into someone's thoughts for a moment.

dig up.example: I ask David, trying to dig up the least little bit of enthusiasm.

draw up.example: All I can think of is to take Shiloh down to Friendly the next day, draw me up a big sign that says free-. world's best dog or something, and hold it up along the road to Sistersville, hoping that some stranger driving along will get a warm spot in his heart for Shiloh, stop his car, and take him home.
draw up.meaning: To make or write out a plan or sign.

go by.example: You've got to go by the law.
go by.meaning: To follow and do what rules say.

good as gold.example: You been good as gold all this time.

in the eyes of the law.example: That doesn't make him yours. Not in the eyes of the law, it doesn't.
in the eyes of the law.meaning: As the law sees it; legally.

kick the daylights out of one.example: You would have thought more of me if I'd let that dog wander around till Judd found it again, kick the daylights out of 'im?

mess with.example: There's the set look about the lips that means trouble--that means don't mess with her, 'cause she's already in trouble with Dad.
mess with.meaning: To bother someone or cross them.

on one's mind.example: You get a dog on your mind, it seems to fill up the whole space.
on one's mind.meaning: In one's thoughts; something one keeps worrying about.

plant oneself.example: Then I'll plant myself on the road to Sistersville, holding that sign, Shiloh waiting beside me wondering what it is we're going to do next.
plant oneself.meaning: To stand or sit firmly in one place.

practice what one preaches.example: The doc's a short man, round belly, don't seem to practice what he preaches about eating right, but he's got a kind heart, and he lays out some newspapers on his kitchen table.
practice what one preaches.meaning: To do what you tell others to do.

put one's mind to.example: How many times you ever put your mind to whether or not it's happy, its ribs sticking out like handles on the sides?

not by a long shot.meaning: No, not at all; far from it.

pull through.meaning: To get better after a bad illness or injury; to live through it.
pull through.example: If you can keep him quiet for a few days and off that leg, I think he'll pull through just fine.

by and by.meaning: After some time; later, in the future.
by and by.example: "I'll get you the money somehow, by and by," I promise.

look the other way.meaning: To pretend not to see something wrong.
look the other way.example: I begin to see now I'm no better than Judd Travers--willing to look the other way to get something I want.

easy as pie.example: Easy as pie for Judd Travers to put a bullet hole in my head, say he didn't see me.

get away with.meaning: To do something wrong without being caught or punished.
get away with.example: But I'm thinkin' straight enough as I help drag that doe to Judd's to know that by lettin' him get away with this, I'm putting other deer in danger.

set up.meaning: To trick someone into a bad or unfair position.
set up.example: Boy, you just come up here to set me up, didn't you?

from ear to ear.meaning: A very big smile, going all the way across the face.
from ear to ear.example: Closer I get to home, though, the bigger the grin on my face, and when I burst in the kitchen, I got a smile from ear to ear.

stick to.meaning: To keep doing what you promised or planned; not to give up.
stick to.example: All I can do is stick to my side of the deal and see what happens.

take to court.meaning: To bring someone before a judge because of a fight over rights or property.
take to court.example: Only way he can get his dog back is to take me to court, and then I'll tell the judge how Judd treats his animals.

take what you can get.meaning: To accept what is offered, even if it is not much.
take what you can get.example: You make a deal with Judd Travers and you're only eleven years old, you take what you can get.

put in one's place.meaning: To speak sharply to someone who is being rude.
put in one's place.example: You think I can't put you in your place mighty quick?

go through with.meaning: To finish something you promised or planned, even when it is hard.
go through with.example: What worries me most is that Judd could go through with the bargain, give Shiloh to me, but then someday, when Shiloh's running free in the woods by himself, Judd might put a bullet in his head, just to spite me.

break one's back.meaning: To work extremely hard, until your body hurts.
break one's back.example: What you breakin' your back for?

shoot off one's mouth.meaning: To talk too much; to brag loudly.
shoot off one's mouth.example: And here I am, shooting off my mouth at five-thirty in the morning to a man holding a rifle.

crack across the mouth.meaning: To hit someone hard on the face.
crack across the mouth.example: Judd Travers is staring at me like he's about to crack me across the mouth.

scrape up.meaning: To gather money or things with great effort, a little at a time.
scrape up.example: Maybe we can scrape up the money to buy him.

go ahead.meaning: To start doing something; to do it with permission.

turn down.meaning: To say no to something offered.
turn down.example: Everything I can think of to try, I've already thought on and turned down.

talk back.meaning: To answer in a rude or unkind way.
talk back.example: Way we're raised around here, children don't talk back to grown folks.

get along.meaning: To live or work together in a friendly way; not to fight.
get along.example: I don't know how we done it, but somehow we learned to get along.

face up to.meaning: To meet something bad or scary without running away.
face up to.example: But it's my story to tell, not Dad's, and he always did make us face up to what we'd done.

let slip.meaning: To tell a secret by accident.
let slip.example: "Who's Shiloh?" she asks, and David realizes he's let it slip.

strike a bargain.meaning: To make a deal or agreement with someone.
strike a bargain.example: Got to have somebody sign that he saw you strike a bargain.

think up.meaning: To make up an idea or an excuse in your head.
think up.example: Don't want to feel that Judd's so sore at me he'll think up any excuse at all to run his truck over my dog.

let out.meaning: To tell a secret; to let people know something hidden.
let out.example: Then I think of how there are exactly seven people now who know I have Judd Travers's dog, and it's only a matter of time before somebody lets it out.

get rid of.meaning: To throw away or remove something unwanted.
get rid of.example: Could be that once he got rid of the evidence, he'd tell me to go ahead and get the warden.

lickety split.example: The beagle comes barreling toward me, legs going lickety-split, long ears flopping, tail sticking up like a flagpole.

paragraphs.context: What do you do when a dog you suspect
paragraphs.mainIdea: The review asks the book's big question: what should you do when a mistreated dog runs to you, but he belongs to someone else -- a man with a gun?
paragraphs.simple: Imagine this: a dog that has been hurt runs away and comes to you for help. But the dog is not yours. The man who owns him has a gun. What would you do? That is the problem Marty faces, and he faces it alone. When he tries to fix it, things get even more frightening. He shows great courage, and he learns that telling right from wrong is not always easy. Still, sometimes a person will do almost anything to save a dog.

paragraphs.context: The day Shiloh come, we're having us a
paragraphs.mainIdea: On the Sunday Shiloh arrived, the family is eating its big midday meal together.
paragraphs.simple: The story begins on the day Shiloh came. The family is eating a big Sunday dinner together at noon. Dara Lynn is dipping her bread into her glass of cold tea, the way she likes to eat it. Becky is pushing her beans up over the edge of her plate, hurrying to get them down fast.

paragraphs.context: there's this shorthaired dog--white with brown and black
paragraphs.mainIdea: By the river, Marty spots a thin, frightened young beagle, slinking along with his tail between his legs.
paragraphs.simple: This afternoon Marty is walking up the road along the river. Out of the corner of his eye he sees something move. About fifteen yards away there is a shorthaired dog, white with brown and black spots. The dog makes no noise. He slinks along with his head down, watching Marty, his tail between his legs, as if he hardly has the right to breathe. He is a beagle, maybe a year or two old.

paragraphs.context: Something really hurts inside you when you see
paragraphs.mainIdea: The way the dog cringes tells Marty that someone has been kicking and beating him.
paragraphs.simple: It hurts inside when you see a dog cringe like that. Marty understands what it means: somebody has been kicking at the dog, maybe beating on him.

paragraphs.context: It's like pressing a magic button. The beagle
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Marty whistles, the beagle comes racing to him, overjoyed, licking his hand and jumping on him.
paragraphs.simple: Marty whistles without thinking. It works like magic. The beagle comes barreling toward him, legs going lickety-split, long ears flopping, tail up like a flagpole. When Marty holds out his hand, the dog licks his fingers and jumps against his leg, making little yelps. The dog cannot get enough of him. Marty is sure now it is a he-dog, as he had thought.

paragraphs.context: Looks like he's fixing to follow me all the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty starts to worry: the dog seems set on following him home, and his family never allowed pets -- coming home wet already means trouble, since his grandmother died of pneumonia.
paragraphs.simple: Once the dog follows Marty across the bridge and past the gristmill, Marty starts to worry. It looks like the dog is about to follow him all the way home. Marty is already in trouble for coming home with wet clothes -- his mother's mother died of pneumonia, and the family never lets him forget it. And now he has a dog with him, and they were never allowed to have pets.

paragraphs.context: If you can't afford to feed 'em and take
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ma's rule: if you cannot afford to feed a pet and take it to the vet when sick, you have no right to take it in.
paragraphs.simple: Ma says this, and Marty knows it is true: if you cannot afford to feed animals and take them to the vet when they are sick, you have no right to take them in.

paragraphs.context: I was in the corner store once down in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty once watched Judd cheat Mr. Wallace: Judd paid with a ten-dollar bill, then claimed he had given a twenty, and the confused old man handed him extra change.
paragraphs.simple: One reason Marty dislikes Judd: he once saw Judd cheat Mr. Wallace at the cash register in the corner store. Judd gave the man a ten, got him talking, and then -- when Mr. Wallace gave him his change -- said he had given him a twenty.

paragraphs.context: Third reason I don't like him is because he
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the fairgrounds, Judd kept getting in front of Marty everywhere -- at the mud bog, the tractor pull, and a motorcycle stunt show.
paragraphs.simple: A third reason Marty dislikes Judd: at the fairgrounds last year, everywhere Marty went, Judd was in front of him, blocking his view. He stood in front of Marty at the mud bog, sat in front of him at the tractor pull, and stood right up out of his seat at the motorcycle globe-of-death act, so Marty missed the best part.

paragraphs.context: he kills deer out of season. He says he
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty once saw a young buck with a bullet hole on Judd's truck, though Judd claimed he had accidentally run over it -- and Marty suspects Judd shoots deer out of season.
paragraphs.simple: A fourth reason: Judd kills deer out of season. He says he does not, but Marty once saw him at dusk with a young buck strapped over the hood of his truck. Judd told him the buck ran in front of him on the road and he accidentally ran over it, but Marty saw the bullet hole himself.

paragraphs.context: If this dog's mistreated, he's only about one out
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dad says one mistreated dog is nothing unusual -- people abandon animals in the hills all the time, expecting them to live on rats and rabbits.
paragraphs.simple: Dad answers that if this dog is mistreated, he is only one of about fifty thousand animals that are. People even bring animals up into the hills and let them out, thinking they can live on rats and rabbits. This would not be the first dog that was not treated right.

paragraphs.context: But this one come to me to help him I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty insists the dog came to him for help, and admits he has become deeply attached to him.
paragraphs.simple: But Marty insists: this dog came to him asking for help. He knew that was why the dog was following him. He has gotten hooked on the dog, Dad, and he wants to know the dog is treated right.

paragraphs.context: Up here in the hills you hardly ever get
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the hills, people never rush to the point: they say hello, chat about other things, and only slowly edge toward what they came to say, so as not to offend.
paragraphs.simple: Judd comes out onto his little porch, and the two men stand and talk for a while. Up here in the hills, Marty explains, you hardly ever get straight down to business. First you say your howdys, then you talk about anything except what you came for, and finally -- when the mosquitoes start to bite -- you say what is on your mind. But you always edge into it gently, so you do not offend.

paragraphs.context: Shiloh leaps off my lap onto the ground and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The moment Judd takes him, Shiloh is kicked, yelps, and runs off with his belly to the ground while the chained dogs bark wildly.
paragraphs.simple: Judd opens the Jeep door and orders the dog down. Before Marty can give him one last pat, Shiloh leaps off his lap onto the ground and runs into Judd's right foot -- a kick. He yelps and runs off behind the trailer, tail tucked down, belly to the ground. All of Judd's dogs, chained out back, bark like crazy.

paragraphs.context: I'll leave him be tonight, but he wanders
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd promises to beat Shiloh badly if the dog wanders off again.
paragraphs.simple: Judd only growls. He says Shiloh could be a fine hunting dog, but the dog tries his patience. He will leave him alone tonight, but if he wanders off again, he will whup the daylights out of him -- beat him very hard. He guarantees it.

paragraphs.context: He drives his Jeep to the post office in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dad's mail route covers about 400 families and some 85 miles of rough roads that are barely passable in winter.
paragraphs.simple: First Dad makes a lunch to carry to work. He drives his Jeep to the post office in Sistersville, where he sorts mail for around two hundred families and delivers it. Then he comes back to the Friendly post office, where he sorts mail for two hundred more families, and delivers that too. His route runs about eighty-five miles, on roads you can hardly get by on in winter.

paragraphs.context: Read once in a book about how some kids
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty does plenty of unpaid work at home and would never ask for pay -- in his house, everyone just does their share.
paragraphs.simple: Marty once read in a book about kids who earned money baby-sitting. He thinks: if he ever got paid even a nickel for every time he took care of Becky and Dara Lynn, he would have a lot of dollars. He does many jobs that other kids get paid for, but it would never occur to him to ask for pay. If he asked Dad, Dad would say, 'You live in this house, boy?' -- and when Marty said yes, Dad would say, 'Then you do your share like the rest of us.'

paragraphs.context: But seeing those bugs in a jar reminds me
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lightning bugs trapped in a jar remind Marty of Shiloh chained at Judd's -- a prisoner, just like them.
paragraphs.simple: Dad laughs at Becky squealing when she catches a bug in her hand. But seeing those bugs in a jar reminds Marty of Shiloh, all chained up at Judd's -- a prisoner as sure as those bugs are. The truth is, almost everything reminds him of Shiloh. Once a dog looks at you the way Shiloh looked at him, you never forget it.

paragraphs.context: Got me a week of vacation coming, so I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd is taking days off work to go hunting with his dogs on the ridge, hoping for rabbit or possum.
paragraphs.simple: Judd says he has a week of vacation coming, so he takes a day off now and then. This Friday he is going hunting again -- taking the dogs up on the ridge to try to get some rabbit, or maybe possum. He has not had a possum dinner for some time.

paragraphs.context: Didn't give him a ounce of supper that night.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd punished Shiloh by giving him no supper and making him watch the other dogs eat.
paragraphs.simple: 'He's learning,' Judd says. He did not give Shiloh an ounce of supper that night. He just put him where he could watch the other dogs eat -- to teach him not to wander off. Right now he has him back in the shed.

paragraphs.context: Never name any of my dogs. Dogs one, two,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd never names his dogs -- he whistles when he wants them and kicks them when he doesn't, calling them 'Git,' 'Scram,' 'Out,' and 'Dammit.'
paragraphs.simple: Judd laughs, and Marty sees his teeth dark with tobacco juice. Judd says his dogs have no names. He never names any of them. They are just dogs one, two, three, and four. When he wants them, he whistles; when he does not, he gives them a kick. 'Git,' 'Scram,' 'Out,' and 'Dammit' -- those are his dogs' names.

paragraphs.context: I was fooling around up on the ridge and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty remembers finding a dead beagle with a bullet hole a year ago, and now wonders if Judd shot one of his own dogs on purpose.
paragraphs.simple: Marty is thinking about a year ago, when he was fooling around up on the ridge and came across a dead dog -- a dead beagle with a hole in its head. He never said anything, because what was there to say? He figured somebody out hunting hit a dog by mistake; it happens. But the more he thinks about it now, the more he wonders if it was Judd Travers shooting a dog on purpose -- shooting one of his own dogs that did not please him.

paragraphs.context: We've got a new game warden in the county,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The county has a tough new game warden who fines people for killing deer illegally -- unlike the old days, when the warden looked the other way.
paragraphs.simple: Dad is still talking. They have a new game warden in the county, and he is plenty tough. It used to be that a man could kill a deer on his own land anytime if the deer was eating his garden, and the warden would look the other way. But the new warden will fine you good. 'Well,' Dad says, 'that is the way it ought to be, I guess.'

paragraphs.context: It isn't that we're rock-poor; trouble is that
paragraphs.mainIdea: The family has no spare money because every extra cent goes to pay for Grandma Preston's nurses.
paragraphs.simple: There are not many leftover scraps in their house -- every extra bite gets made into soup. It is not that they are rock-poor. The trouble is that Grandma Preston has grown real feeble, and Dad's sister is caring for her over in Clarksburg. They have to hire nurses whenever Aunt Hettie goes out, and every spare cent goes to pay for Grandma's care. Nothing is left over to feed a dog.

paragraphs.context: I hear this far-off sound again, like a dog
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lying awake at night, Marty hears a far-off crying sound and wonders with an aching chest if it is Shiloh.
paragraphs.simple: Marty wonders if, in time, he might forget about Shiloh if he never sees him again. But then, lying on the couch that night after everyone else has gone to bed, he hears the far-off sound again -- like a dog crying. Not barking, not howling, not even whining. Crying. He gets an awful ache in his chest. He wonders if it is a dog. If it is Shiloh.

paragraphs.context: Soon as I see him, I know two things:
paragraphs.mainIdea: Seeing Shiloh under the sycamore, Marty understands he ran away while Judd is hunting -- and decides he will never take him back.
paragraphs.simple: Marty goes out the front door. Shiloh is under the sycamore tree, head on his paws, just like the day he followed Marty home in the rain. As soon as Marty sees him, he knows two things: first, Judd Travers has taken his dogs out hunting, as he said he would, and Shiloh has run away from the pack; second, Marty is not going to take him back. Not now, not ever.

paragraphs.context: I know that if I was to see Judd
paragraphs.mainIdea: Carrying Shiloh into the woods, Marty feels he would tell Judd to shoot him first before letting him near the dog again.
paragraphs.simple: Marty whispers Shiloh's name and gathers him up in his arms. The dog's body is shaking all over, but he does not try to get away. Marty holds him as carefully as he carries Becky when she is asleep, and starts up the far hill into the woods, carrying his dog. He knows that if he saw Judd Travers that very minute with his rifle, he would tell him he would have to shoot Marty first before he ever let him near Shiloh again.

paragraphs.context: I'd made a promise to Judd Travers I wasn't
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty admits he broke his promise to Judd -- but he makes Shiloh a stronger promise that he will keep.
paragraphs.simple: The way Shiloh looks at him and licks his face seals the promise. Marty had made a promise to Judd Travers that he was not going to keep -- Jesus help him. But now he is making a promise to Shiloh that he will keep, God strike him dead.

paragraphs.context: Like he had the bark beat out of him when
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shiloh stays silent, and Marty thinks it is because the bark was beaten out of him as a puppy.
paragraphs.simple: Marty puts his finger to his lips and says, 'Shhh!' all the way down the hill. Shiloh does not make a sound. It is as if he had the bark beat out of him when he was a pup, and it just never came back.

paragraphs.context: No one looks up. No one pauses. No one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nobody at the table notices Marty's trick -- saving meat loaf for Shiloh works easily.
paragraphs.simple: The forks keep clinking on the table. Becky keeps digging her fork into her boiled potato. No one looks up. No one pauses. No one even asks a question. Fooling them is easy as falling off a log.

paragraphs.context: Ain't looking for a meal, Mrs. Preston, I'm looking
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd arrives in the evening, not for dinner but to look for his missing dog -- and Marty's heart pounds.
paragraphs.simple: Judd says he already had ribs; he is not looking for a meal. He is looking for a dog. He does not waste any time getting to the point. Now Marty's heart is really pounding.

paragraphs.context: I swear to God I find him this time, I'm
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd threatens to break the dog's legs if he finds him this time.
paragraphs.simple: Judd spits and swears: if he finds the dog this time, he is going to break his legs.

paragraphs.context: Whup him good and starve him lean. Wondered if
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd says the runaway dog is no use to him, and plans to beat and starve him as a lesson.
paragraphs.simple: Judd says a dog with four broken legs would be no dog to him at all -- but the dog is no use to him anyway, the way he keeps running off. It is the fourth time he has left the pack while hunting. Judd says he has to teach him a lesson: beat him good and starve him lean.

paragraphs.context: Haven't seen any dog of any kind in our
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty tells Judd he hasn't seen any dog in the yard all day -- true about the yard, but hiding that he has seen Shiloh.
paragraphs.simple: Marty stands rooted to the ground. 'His dog? Here in this yard?' he asks. 'I haven't seen any dog of any kind in our yard all day,' he says, coming a few steps closer.

paragraphs.context: but Jesus knows. And right this very minute Jesus is looking down
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ma tells Marty that Jesus knows who ate the candy rabbit's ear, and that being cut off from God's love is the worst thing that can happen.
paragraphs.simple: Ma says Dara Lynn and she do not know who ate the ear off the candy rabbit, but Jesus knows. She says the worst thing that can ever happen to us is to be kept away from God's love forever, and Marty should keep that in mind.

paragraphs.context: you can lie not only by what you say but what you don't say
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty realizes he has lied to Judd not by what he said, but by what he kept quiet.
paragraphs.simple: Marty did not tell a direct lie to Judd, because Shiloh had not been near the yard. But he also did not tell the whole truth, so Judd thinks Marty never saw the dog at all. Marty sees that keeping quiet can be a lie too.

paragraphs.context: Be one hundred percent honest and carry that dog back to Judd
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty prays to Jesus, asking if he should tell the whole truth and return Shiloh to be hurt again, or keep the dog and feed him.
paragraphs.simple: Marty asks Jesus what he wants him to do. If Marty is one hundred percent honest, he must take Shiloh back to Judd, where one of God's creatures will be kicked and starved all over again. If he keeps Shiloh, he can feed him and keep him safe. He does not know which choice is right.

paragraphs.context: Every bit of food saved is money saved that could go to buy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty secretly gives his own food to Shiloh, and tries to tell himself there is no harm in it.
paragraphs.simple: Marty is also lying to his parents by not eating the food he saves for Shiloh. Every bit of food saved is money saved, and the family needs money for Dara Lynn's new shoes, a telephone, and Grandma Preston's care. But he tells himself that if it is food from his own plate that he would have eaten himself, there is no harm in it.

paragraphs.context: Funny how one lie leads to another and before you know it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty lies to his parents about why David should not visit, and sees that one lie keeps leading to more lies.
paragraphs.simple: Marty tells his parents there is nothing for David Howard to do at their house, but that is a flat-out lie. He sees that one lie leads to another, and before he knows it, his whole life can become a lie.

paragraphs.context: Pa took the belt to me--big old welts on my back so raw
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd tells Marty that his father used to beat him badly when he was little, and he stayed because he had nowhere else to go.
paragraphs.simple: Judd says that as far back as he can remember, when he was four, his father hit him with a belt. The marks on his back were so bad that he could hardly pull his shirt on. He did not run away because he had no other place to go.

paragraphs.context: You see him, just whistle, then hang on to him and I'll come
paragraphs.mainIdea: Judd tells Marty how to catch Shiloh: whistle in the fields, hold the dog, and wait for Judd to come get him.
paragraphs.simple: Judd says Shiloh is a shy dog who stays in the fields, not near the roads. If Marty sees him, all he has to do is whistle. Judd trained the dog to come to his whistle to be fed. Marty should hold the dog until Judd comes to pick him up. Judd also says that if the dog does something he does not like, he kicks him very hard.

paragraphs.context: Has four bedrooms upstairs: one for David, one for his folks
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty describes David Howard's big house, which has whole rooms set aside just for guests, books, and plants.
paragraphs.simple: David's house is much bigger than Marty's, though fewer people live in it. It has two floors, plus a basement and an attic. Upstairs there are four bedrooms: one for David, one for his parents, one only for company, and one only for his father's books, with a computer in it. Downstairs there is a dining room, a parlor, and a side room only for plants, with a porch running along three sides of the house.

paragraphs.context: so I figure it'll get to be David's someday
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty thinks David's house will belong to David someday, just as the little house, the hill, the meadow, and the far woods might someday belong to him and Shiloh.
paragraphs.simple: David says the house used to belong to his great-grandfather, so Marty thinks it will belong to David someday. In the same way, maybe their little house, the hill, the meadow, and the far woods will belong to Marty and Shiloh -- though Marty would have to share them with Dara Lynn, Becky, and the men they marry, and that is a whole lot of people for four rooms.

paragraphs.context: I expect something warm and wiggly and furry to plop into
paragraphs.mainIdea: David's surprise pet turns out to be a hermit crab in a fishbowl, not the warm, furry animal Marty expected.
paragraphs.simple: Marty sits down, closes his eyes, and holds out his hands. He expects something warm and wiggly and furry to fall into his arms. Instead he feels something cold and round and plastic. When he looks, he sees a fishbowl with sand in it and a hermit crab with a shell on its back, moving around. It is David's first pet, and its name is Hermie.

paragraphs.context: A lie don't seem a lie anymore when it's meant to save a dog
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty admits he will do almost anything for Shiloh, and lying no longer feels like lying when it is meant to save the dog.
paragraphs.simple: Marty eats the tapioca pudding himself because he cannot carry it to Shiloh, but he takes six cookies for the walk home. He knows his mother would be ashamed to hear him ask for extra food. Still, he will do almost anything for Shiloh now. A lie does not seem like a lie to him anymore when it is meant to save a dog, and right and wrong are all mixed up in his head.

paragraphs.context: I got some stuff here that's not exactly spoiled, but it's too old
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Wallace sells Marty old cheese, sour cream, and frankfurters for his fifty-three cents, acting as if he does not want to embarrass him.
paragraphs.simple: Marty asks Mr. Wallace for cheap old cheese or meat. Mr. Wallace takes him into the little room behind the counter. He talks without looking at Marty, the way people do when they do not want to make someone feel bad. He sells Marty a big piece of cheese with mold on one side, a carton of sour cream, and half a pack of frankfurters for all the change Marty has. He says the food is not really spoiled, just too old to sell.

paragraphs.context: set it in the cool stream, surround it with rocks, and put the container
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty hides Shiloh's food in a can set in the cool stream so it will not spoil in the July heat.
paragraphs.simple: Marty cannot keep the food in the house refrigerator, or his mother would see it right away. He takes an old Hi-C can up the hill. With Shiloh watching, he puts a rock in the bottom of the can to hold it down, sets it in the cool stream, surrounds it with rocks, and puts the sour cream, frankfurters, cheese, and cookies inside. He puts the lid on and a large rock on top to keep the raccoons out.

paragraphs.context: and liars go to hell, then I guess that's where I'm headed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty thinks his lies may send him to hell, but he would leave heaven anyway if Shiloh were not there with him.
paragraphs.simple: Marty does not feel good about the lies he tells Dara Lynn, David, and David's mother, but he does not feel completely bad either. His grandmother told him that liars go to hell, and that only people, not animals, are allowed in heaven. Marty thinks he is probably headed to hell. But even if he went to heaven and looked down to see Shiloh left below with his head on his paws, he would run away from heaven for sure.

paragraphs.context: Having Shiloh a secret is like a bomb waiting to go off
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty fears Judd only wants to hunt on their land to look for his dog, and keeping Shiloh a secret feels dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: Dad says he will tell Judd no about hunting on their land. Marty stops gripping his chair, but his heart keeps beating hard. He thinks Judd may believe the dog is hidden up on the hill and is looking for an excuse to snoop around. Keeping Shiloh a secret feels like a bomb waiting to go off.

paragraphs.context: had I seen him, and I said I hadn't seen him in our yard
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty explains the tricky half-truth he told Judd.
paragraphs.simple: Judd asked Marty if he had seen the dog. Marty only said he had not seen the dog in their yard. That much was true, because the dog was hidden up on the hill, not in the yard. But Marty was hiding the full truth.

paragraphs.context: "So we've got ourselves a secret," she says at last,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ma decides to share Marty's secret for now.
paragraphs.simple: Ma has found the dog and Marty's hiding place. She does not yell at him. She says the two of them now have a secret together. Hearing her say "we" makes Marty feel a little better.

paragraphs.context: you to eat more'n a couple bites of squash in your life
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ma explains how the squash gave Marty away.
paragraphs.simple: Ma knows Marty almost never eats squash. When he saved a spoonful to eat later, she knew the food was for the hidden dog. Then she noticed him sneaking off every night.

paragraphs.context: what kind of law is it, Ma, that lets a man mistreat his dog?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty questions whether the law is fair.
paragraphs.simple: Ma says the law gives the dog to Judd, not to Marty. Marty asks how a law can be right if it lets a man be cruel to his dog.

paragraphs.context: If I keep this one secret from him, he'll think maybe there are more.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ma explains why she must tell Dad.
paragraphs.simple: Ma says she has kept no secrets from Dad in fourteen years of marriage. If she hides this one secret, Dad may stop trusting her and think she hides more.

paragraphs.context: Judd Travers ever comes here to get his dog, he'll have to fight me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty swears he will fight Judd for the dog.
paragraphs.simple: Marty is crying and angry. He tells Ma that if Judd comes to take Shiloh, Judd will have to fight him first.

paragraphs.context: Judd won't sell me Shiloh's spit for a nickel.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty has almost no money left to buy Shiloh.
paragraphs.simple: Marty spent all his can money on dog food. All he has left is a nickel he found by the road. Judd would not sell even the dog's spit for a nickel, so he will never sell Shiloh that cheap.

paragraphs.context: All I can think of is to take Shiloh down to Friendly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty plans to give Shiloh to a stranger by the road.
paragraphs.simple: Marty thinks of taking Shiloh to the road to Sistersville with a sign that says the dog is free. He hopes a kind stranger will stop and take Shiloh home. Then he can honestly tell Ma he does not know where the dog is.

paragraphs.context: I feel like there's a tank truck sitting on my chest; can't hardly breathe.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty feels crushed by his hard choice.
paragraphs.simple: Marty worries he might give Shiloh to someone even worse than Judd. Thinking about it feels like a heavy truck is sitting on his chest, and he can hardly breathe.

paragraphs.context: this big German shepherd, mean as nails, hunched over Shiloh there on the ground.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty finds a German shepherd attacking Shiloh.
paragraphs.simple: Dad shines the flashlight, and Marty sees a big German shepherd standing over Shiloh on the ground. The big dog has blood on its mouth. When Dad steps closer, it jumps over the fence and runs into the woods.

paragraphs.context: He's dead, I know it! I'm screaming inside.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty thinks Shiloh is dead.
paragraphs.simple: Shiloh lies still and does not move. Marty is sure the dog is dead. He is crying loudly inside himself, without making a sound. Then he feels Shiloh's body shiver a little.

paragraphs.context: The next twenty-four hours, we'll know if this dog's going to live,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doc Murphy warns Shiloh may not survive.
paragraphs.simple: The doctor says he will do what he can. The big worry now is infection. They will know in the next twenty-four hours if the dog will live. He will keep Shiloh for a day or two.

paragraphs.context: Hardest thing in the world is to leave Shiloh there at Doc Murphy's,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty hates leaving Shiloh with the doctor.
paragraphs.simple: The hardest thing for Marty is to leave Shiloh at the doctor's house. Shiloh's eyes follow Marty to the door, and his body moves like he is trying to get up. The second hardest thing is getting into the Jeep with Dad.

paragraphs.context: not all so black and white as Dad makes it out to be, neither
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty feels the right choice is not clear.
paragraphs.simple: Dad says lying is wrong. But Marty thinks this is not a simple right-or-wrong choice. When he gets angry, his thinking becomes clearer.

paragraphs.context: The law says a man that pays money for a dog owns that dog.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dad says they must follow the law.
paragraphs.simple: Dad says they have to go by the law. The law says the man who paid money for the dog owns it. If Marty does not like the law, he should work to change it.

paragraphs.context: Open up your eyes, Marty. Open your eyes!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dad says cruelty to animals is common.
paragraphs.simple: Dad tells Marty that Judd is not the only person who is cruel to animals. Many dogs are chained up, hungry, and hurt. Marty only wants to change things now because this one dog touched his heart.

paragraphs.context: I'm going to pay Doc Murphy's bill. I promise you that.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty promises to pay for the doctor.
paragraphs.simple: Marty begs Dad to let him keep Shiloh until the dog is well. He promises to pay the doctor's bill with his can money for three years and by delivering the county paper.

paragraphs.context: Worst of all, I'd brought Shiloh here to keep him from being hurt,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty blames himself for the attack.
paragraphs.simple: Marty feels guilty. He brought Shiloh to the hill to keep the dog from being hurt, but the German shepherd hurt Shiloh worse than Judd ever would. He cannot stop crying.

paragraphs.context: want to talk to Dara Lynn, to Becky, to Dad, or even to Ma
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty wants to be alone with his worry.
paragraphs.simple: Marty usually feels lonely at home, but today he wants to stay with that lonely feeling. He does not want to talk to anyone. He is waiting for news about Shiloh.

paragraphs.context: there are exactly seven people now who know I have Judd Travers's dog
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty knows seven people now know his secret, and it is only a matter of time before someone tells. He has learned that the harder a little kid tries to keep a secret, the faster it comes out.
paragraphs.simple: Now seven people know that I have Judd Travers's dog. It is only a matter of time before one of them tells someone else. It will probably be Becky. She will tell the first person who comes up the road. Have you seen how the harder a little kid tries not to tell a secret, the faster the secret comes out? The child cannot stop it. A secret is too big for a little kid to hold.

paragraphs.context: it's my duty to report a killed doe
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty knows it is his duty to report the dead deer, but where he lives that would be called snitching. If he says he might tell, but then agrees to stay quiet in return for Shiloh, that is blackmail.
paragraphs.simple: In one way, it is my duty to report the killed doe. That is the right thing to do. But the way folks up here look at it, that is snitching -- telling on someone. And if I might tell, but I agree not to in return for Shiloh, that is something else again: blackmail. But I have got to the place where I would do almost anything to save Shiloh.

paragraphs.context: I'm no better than Judd Travers--willing to look the other way
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty sees that he is no better than Judd: he is willing to let Judd get away with a wrong thing in order to get what he wants. But the thing he wants is Shiloh.
paragraphs.simple: Now I see I am no better than Judd Travers. I am willing to look the other way -- to let him do a wrong thing -- so I can get what I want. But the thing I want is Shiloh.

paragraphs.context: To save Shiloh, I'm making it harder for deer
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty knows that by helping Judd hide the dead deer, he is putting other deer in danger. Still, when he thinks of Shiloh's face, he keeps on with the job.
paragraphs.simple: Judd killed this deer out of season. He will think now that he can kill more deer too. To save Shiloh, I am making things harder for the deer. I know this, and I swallow hard. But all I have to do is think of how Shiloh would look at me if I ever gave him back to Judd, and then I get on with my work.

paragraphs.context: that's lying by omission, Ma says: not telling the whole truth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty does not want to lie anymore, but hiding the deer story from his parents is also a kind of lie. He keeps his promise to Judd because Shiloh matters most to him now.
paragraphs.simple: I really do not want to lie anymore. If I tell Ma and Dad everything but the deer, that is lying by omission -- not telling the whole truth. But if I tell about the deer after I promised Judd I would not, then I lied to Judd. I would rather lie to Judd than to my parents. But Dad would not report Judd even if he saw him shoot a doe out of season, because that is the way it has always been around here. That does not make it right, but telling him would change nothing. Because I promised not to, I don't. Right now the most important thing to me is Shiloh.

paragraphs.context: Wonder if Dad wouldn't never tell on Judd no matter what he done
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty wonders whether his dad would ever report Judd, no matter what Judd did. He thinks there must be times when one person's actions are everybody's business.
paragraphs.simple: I wonder if Dad would never tell on Judd, no matter what he did. I bet he would tell sometime. There has got to be times when what one person does is everybody's business.

paragraphs.context: how Judd could only remember hunting, well, that was pretty pitiful
paragraphs.mainIdea: For the first time, Marty feels a little sorry for Judd Travers. When Marty thinks of all the things he did with his own dad, and how Judd can only remember hunting, that seems like a very sad life.
paragraphs.simple: I suppose there was only a very small bit of sorry for him inside me. When I thought of all the things I had done with my own dad, and how Judd could only remember hunting, well, that was pretty pitiful for a lifetime.

paragraphs.context: nothing is as simple as you guess--not right or wrong
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marty thinks that nothing is as simple as it looks -- not right or wrong, not Judd, not even himself or Shiloh. But he saved Shiloh and he sees things more clearly now.
paragraphs.simple: I look at the dark closing in. The sky gets more and more purple. I am thinking how nothing is as simple as you guess. Not right or wrong. Not Judd Travers. Not even me, or this dog I have here. But the good part is I saved Shiloh, and I opened my eyes some. Now that is not bad for eleven.

sentences.context: When it is someone else's dog? When the man
sentences.grammar: These short questions finish the first question 'What do you do when...?'; read them as 'What do you do when it is someone else's dog?' and 'What do you do when the man who owns him has a gun?'
sentences.simple: The big question keeps going: what do you do when the dog belongs to someone else? What do you do when the owner is a man with a gun?

sentences.context: The day Shiloh come, we're having us a
sentences.grammar: 'come' is the dialect past of 'came'; 'having us a big dinner' just means 'having a big dinner' -- the extra 'us' adds a warm, friendly feel.
sentences.simple: On the day Shiloh came, we are eating a big Sunday dinner.

sentences.context: He don't even whimper, like he's lost his
sentences.grammar: In this dialect 'don't' is used with 'he' too; standard English uses 'doesn't'.
sentences.simple: He does not even whimper, as if he has lost his bark.

sentences.context: I can see his ribs--not real bad--but he
sentences.grammar: 'real' is used for 'very' here; 'plumped out' means fat and well-fed (see the phrase card).
sentences.simple: I can see his ribs -- it is not very bad -- but he is not fat and healthy either.

sentences.context: Don't know where you'd end up if you
sentences.grammar: The opening 'I' is dropped, as in quick speech; read it as 'I don't know...'.
sentences.simple: I do not know where you would end up if you followed the river all the way.

sentences.context: Looks like he's fixing to follow me all
sentences.grammar: The opening 'It' is dropped; 'fixing to' is dialect for 'about to' (see the phrase card).
sentences.simple: It looks like he is about to follow me all the way to our house.

sentences.context: he probably don't have sense enough yet to
sentences.grammar: 'don't' is used for 'doesn't' in this dialect; 'sense enough' means 'enough sense' -- 'enough' comes after the noun.
sentences.simple: He probably does not have enough sense yet to find his way home again.

sentences.context: you wouldn't feel no pull for keeping an
sentences.grammar: Double negative for emphasis: 'wouldn't feel no pull' means 'wouldn't feel any pull'.
sentences.simple: Wouldn't you feel something pulling you to keep watching him?

sentences.context: all the way home I can't speak a word,
sentences.grammar: 'trying to hold the tears back' tells what he was doing while he could not speak -- he was fighting back tears.
sentences.simple: All the way home I cannot say a word, because I am trying not to cry.

sentences.context: Route takes him 'bout eighty-five miles on roads
sentences.grammar: 'bout' is 'about'; the sentence ends with 'on' because 'roads' is what you 'get by on' -- 'roads you can hardly get by on'.
sentences.simple: His route covers about eighty-five miles of roads that are barely passable in winter.

sentences.context: Thinking don't cost nothing," I tell her.
sentences.grammar: Double negative: 'don't cost nothing' means 'doesn't cost anything'; 'don't' is used with a singular subject in this dialect.
sentences.simple: Thinking does not cost anything, I tell her.

sentences.context: reminds me of Shiloh all chained up at
sentences.grammar: 'all chained up' describes Shiloh's state; 'a prisoner as sure as those bugs' means 'as much a prisoner as the bugs are'.
sentences.simple: Seeing the bugs in the jar makes me think of Shiloh, chained up at Judd's -- as much a prisoner as those bugs.

sentences.context: I stuff the mail in, turn up the little
sentences.grammar: The second 'I' is dropped after 'and'; read it as 'and I turn up...'.
sentences.simple: I push the mail into the box and lift the little red flag on its side.

sentences.context: Got me a week of vacation coming, so I
sentences.grammar: The opening 'I' is dropped; 'Got me' is dialect for 'I have'.
sentences.simple: I have got a week of vacation coming, so I am taking a day off now and then.

sentences.context: Dogs one, two, three, and four is all.
sentences.grammar: 'is' is used with a plural subject in this dialect; standard English uses 'are'.
sentences.simple: Dogs one, two, three, and four -- that is all of their names.

sentences.context: it's his dog, not yours, and put your
sentences.grammar: The second 'you've got to' is left out; it applies to both parts: 'you've got to get it through your head... and (you've got to) put your mind to other things'.
sentences.simple: You must understand that it is his dog, not yours, and you must think about other things.

sentences.context: Well, son, you got to try.
sentences.grammar: 'you got to' is short for 'you have got to', meaning 'you must'.
sentences.simple: Well, son, you have got to try -- you must try.

sentences.context: up on the ridge and come across a
sentences.grammar: 'come across' is used as the past tense here; standard English uses 'came across'.
sentences.simple: Up on the ridge I came across a dead dog -- I found one by chance.

sentences.context: trouble is that Grandma Preston's got real feeble
sentences.grammar: 'trouble is that...' is short for 'the trouble is that...'; 'got feeble' means 'became weak'; 'real' means 'very'.
sentences.simple: The trouble is that Grandma Preston has become very weak.

sentences.context: I fold the bread up, jelly to the inside, stick
sentences.grammar: The repeated 'I' is dropped before 'stick' (and 'go'); 'jelly to the inside' means the jelly side is folded inward.
sentences.simple: I fold the bread with the jelly side inside, put it in my pocket, and go out the front door.

sentences.context: I know that if I was to see Judd
sentences.grammar: 'if I was to see' imagines something untrue; standard English often uses 'if I were to see'.
sentences.simple: I know that if I were to see Judd Travers at that very moment with his rifle...

sentences.context: Judd Travers isn't never going to kick you
sentences.grammar: Double negative for strong feeling: 'isn't never' means 'is never' / 'will never'.
sentences.simple: Judd Travers is never going to kick you again -- never.

sentences.context: I'd made a promise to Judd Travers I wasn't
sentences.grammar: 'Jesus help me' is a short prayer: 'may Jesus help me'.
sentences.simple: I had made a promise to Judd Travers that I was not going to keep -- God help me.

sentences.context: Like he had the bark beat out of him
sentences.grammar: 'Like' here means 'as if'; 'come back' is the dialect past of 'came back' (see the phrase card for 'beat out of').
sentences.simple: It is as if the bark was beaten out of him when he was a puppy, and it never came back.

sentences.context: for a while we both lay there, panting, enjoying
sentences.grammar: 'lay' here is the past of 'lie' (to rest flat); 'panting, enjoying...' describe what they were doing while lying there.
sentences.simple: For a while we both lay there in the sun, breathing hard and enjoying it, feeling that we belonged to each other.

sentences.context: I been getting this sort of full feeling at
sentences.grammar: 'I been' is short for 'I have been' -- the 'have' is dropped.
sentences.simple: I have been getting a sort of full feeling at dinner, Ma.

sentences.context: Don't you go pickin' at it.
sentences.grammar: 'go pickin'' means 'start picking' or 'keep picking'; 'pick at' food means taking small bits of it.
sentences.simple: Do not start taking little bits of it.

sentences.context: Think I'll take my .22 and go up the
sentences.grammar: The opening 'I' is dropped; read it as 'I think...'.
sentences.simple: I think I will take my rifle and go up the far hill for a while.

sentences.context: What you figure on shooting this time of
sentences.grammar: The 'do' is dropped ('What do you...'); 'figure on shooting' means 'plan to shoot'.
sentences.simple: What do you plan to shoot at this time of evening?

sentences.context: Don't you ever, never, aim your gun toward
sentences.grammar: 'ever, never' doubles the negative for a very strong warning: 'never ever'.
sentences.simple: Do not ever aim your gun toward this house or yard -- never.

sentences.context: He sure don't waste any time getting to the
sentences.grammar: 'don't' is used with 'he' in this dialect (standard: 'doesn't'); 'getting to the point' means starting the real matter.
sentences.simple: He certainly does not waste any time starting his real business.

sentences.context: Haven't seen any dog of any kind in our
sentences.grammar: The opening 'I' is dropped; read it as 'I haven't seen...'.
sentences.simple: I have not seen any dog of any kind in our yard all day.

sentences.context: I wouldn't never promise him that
sentences.grammar: Double negative: in this dialect, "wouldn't never" means "would never" (standard English uses only one negative).
sentences.simple: I would never promise him that.

sentences.context: there ain't no street lamps at all
sentences.grammar: Double negative: "ain't no" means "are no" here; standard English says "there are no street lamps at all."
sentences.simple: There are no street lamps at all where I live.

sentences.context: About an hour later she come out on the porch
sentences.grammar: Dialect verb form: "come" is used as the past tense; standard English says "she came out."
sentences.simple: About an hour later she came out onto the porch.

sentences.context: "Jesus," I whisper finally, "which you want me to do?
sentences.grammar: Dialect question: the helper verb "do" is left out; standard English is "Which do you want me to do?"
sentences.simple: "Jesus," I whisper finally, "which do you want me to do?"

sentences.context: Repeat it to myself so's to remember it in case I need
sentences.grammar: "So's" is short for "so as"; it means "in order to," so the phrase means "so that I remember it."
sentences.simple: I repeat it to myself so that I will remember it in case I need it.

sentences.context: What pleases you one day don't please you at all the next.
sentences.grammar: Dialect verb form: "don't" is used with a singular subject; standard English uses "doesn't."
sentences.simple: What pleases you one day does not please you at all the next day.

sentences.context: "Eleven's got about everything on its mind," Ma answers.
sentences.grammar: "Eleven's" here means "eleven-year-olds"; a possessive-like form is used as a plural subject.
sentences.simple: "Eleven-year-olds have almost everything on their minds," Ma answers.

sentences.context: Nobody ever felt sorry for me, and I never felt sorry for nobody else.
sentences.grammar: Double negative: "never ... nobody else" means "never anybody at all" in this dialect.
sentences.simple: Nobody ever felt sorry for me, and I never felt sorry for anybody at all.

sentences.context: and how the county's going to be better because of it, and so will
sentences.grammar: Short form with "so": "and so will the whole state" means "and the whole state will be better too."
sentences.simple: And the county is going to be better because of it, and the whole state of West Virginia will be better too.

sentences.context: How many snakes you figure are up there, Marty?
sentences.grammar: Dialect question: "do" is left out; standard English is "How many snakes do you figure are up there?"
sentences.simple: How many snakes do you think are up there, Marty?

sentences.context: Wasn't a thing I bought that wasn't on sale.
sentences.grammar: Double negative: "wasn't a thing ... that wasn't on sale" means "everything was on sale."
sentences.simple: Everything I bought was on sale.

sentences.context: had I seen him, and I said I hadn't seen him in our yard
sentences.grammar: The 'if' or 'whether' is left out of the reported question: 'He asked had I seen him' means 'He asked if I had seen him.'
sentences.simple: Judd asked whether I had seen the dog, and I said I had not seen him in our yard.

sentences.context: This dog don't belong to you.
sentences.grammar: Dialect: 'don't' is used for 'doesn't' with a third-person subject ('this dog doesn't').
sentences.simple: This dog does not belong to you. He is not yours.

sentences.context: You ain't going to tell him?
sentences.grammar: Dialect: 'ain't' stands for 'aren't' or 'isn't' in this question.
sentences.simple: You are not going to tell him, are you?

sentences.context: and he don't move. Not an inch.
sentences.grammar: Dialect: 'don't' is used for 'doesn't' with 'he.' 'Not an inch' is a short, broken-off fragment used for strong feeling.
sentences.simple: And he does not move at all -- not even a tiny bit.

sentences.context: both hands on him so's he won't try to get up.
sentences.grammar: Dialect: 'so's' is a short form of 'so that' or 'so he will.'
sentences.simple: I keep both hands on him so that he will not try to get up.

sentences.context: more of me if I'd let that dog wander around till Judd found it
sentences.grammar: A counterfactual question about the past: 'would have thought' plus 'if I'd let' imagines a different past and asks Dad to judge it.
sentences.simple: You would have respected me more if I had let the dog wander until Judd found it again and beat it badly?

sentences.context: Shiloh's still alive, and I ain't licked yet.
sentences.grammar: Dialect 'ain't' for 'am not.' 'Licked' is old slang for beaten or defeated.
sentences.simple: Shiloh is still alive, and I am not beaten yet.

sentences.context: told you I just found out about that dog myself
sentences.grammar: Overheard broken speech: the words come with gaps and missing starts, so Marty hears only pieces of his parents' talk.
sentences.simple: I just found out about that dog myself, I tell you.

sentences.context: You don't agree with the law, then you work to change it.
sentences.grammar: An order used as a condition: 'You don't agree..., then you...' means the same as 'If you don't agree..., then....'
sentences.simple: If you do not agree with the law, work to change it.

sentences.context: Can it be he knows what I'm fixing to do?
sentences.grammar: An inverted wondering question ('Can it be...?'), plus dialect 'fixing to' meaning 'about to.'
sentences.simple: Could it be that he knows what I am about to do?

sentences.context: Judd Travers ever comes here to get his dog, he'll have to fight me
sentences.grammar: Dialect: 'ever' at the start of the clause works like 'whenever' or 'if ever.'
sentences.simple: If Judd Travers ever comes here to take his dog, he will have to fight me first.

sentences.context: Ma says Jesus don't go around making anyone blind
sentences.simple: Ma says Jesus does not go around making people blind.
sentences.grammar: In standard English, 'he', 'she', and 'it' take "doesn't", not "don't". In Marty's dialect, "don't" is used for everyone.

sentences.context: how the more a little kid tries not to tell a secret, the sooner
sentences.simple: Have you noticed that the harder a small child tries to keep a secret, the faster the secret comes out?
sentences.grammar: "The more ... the sooner ..." is a pattern meaning "when one thing grows, the other grows too": more trying to hide the secret = sooner telling it.

sentences.context: Think it's going to take a couple weeks to heal
sentences.simple: I think it will take a couple of weeks to heal.
sentences.grammar: The subject "I" is left out, as people often do in quick speech: "(I) think it's going to take ..."

sentences.context: Wouldn't never have happened if you'd brought him back like I told you
sentences.simple: It would never have happened if you had brought him back as I told you.
sentences.grammar: "Wouldn't never" is a double negative. In this dialect two negatives make one strong negative, meaning "would never".

sentences.context: we let Shiloh out one day and he never come back
sentences.simple: ... and I will tell Judd that we let Shiloh out one day and he never came back.
sentences.grammar: "Come" is used here for the past tense. Standard English uses "came": "he never came back."

sentences.context: that paper's not good for anything but to blow your nose on
sentences.simple: That paper is good for nothing except blowing your nose on it.
sentences.grammar: The preposition "on" is left at the end of the sentence. The thing it points to ("that paper") comes first, so "on" has nothing after it.

sentences.context: how things would have turned out if it hadn't been for that deer
sentences.simple: I wonder what would have happened without that deer.
sentences.grammar: "Would have turned out if it hadn't been" talks about an unreal past. It did happen, but Marty imagines a past in which it did not.

sentences.context: Your dog come over here twice because you been mistreatin' it
sentences.simple: Your dog came over here twice because you have been mistreating it.
sentences.grammar: "Come" stands for the past "came", and "been" stands for "have been". The helper "have" is dropped in this dialect.

sentences.context: I can't hardly believe the words that's coming out of my mouth
sentences.simple: I can hardly believe the words that are coming out of my mouth.
sentences.grammar: "Can't hardly" is a double negative meaning "can hardly". "That's" is used here for the plural "that are".

sentences.context: I lay out there on my back in the grass
sentences.simple: I lie out there on my back in the grass, not caring about the dew.
sentences.grammar: "Lay" is used here for "lie" (to rest flat). Standard English uses "lie" for a person resting: "I lie on my back."

sentences.context: you ever tell anyone, even your ma and dad, may Jesus make you blind
sentences.simple: If you ever tell anyone, I hope Jesus makes you blind.
sentences.grammar: "May Jesus make you blind" is an old curse formula. "May" + a name + a verb makes a strong wish, good or bad.

sentences.context: you can tell he ain't got that much practice being kind
sentences.simple: You can see he does not have much practice being kind.
sentences.grammar: "Ain't" is dialect for "isn't", "aren't", or "hasn't". Here it means "has not": "he has not got much practice."
